paragraphs: The paper tackles two learning problems together: estimating a model's probabilities and discovering which hidden relationships the model needs. It starts with an oversized random model and uses an entropy-based prior to favor informative, less ambiguous probability assignments. Learning therefore determines both the values of the parameters and the structure that survives.

The estimator balances agreement with the data against uncertainty in the model and the data's descriptive statistics. Parameters with weak support gradually disappear, making the representation smaller and sparser. Additional trimming operations speed up this simplification. Their distinctive property is that removing parameters is guaranteed to increase posterior probability, tying simplification directly to the Bayesian learning objective.

Applied to hidden Markov models, the approach produces compact state machines for music, handwriting, and video sequences. The reported surviving states align with meaningful divisions in the data, while transitions capture predictable dynamics. These findings suggest that compression can help expose interpretable temporal structure while preserving the model's ability to predict.
neurips-1998-an-entropic-estimator-for-s.tldr: An entropy-based learning method simplifies oversized probabilistic models into compact structures that capture meaningful temporal relationships.

paragraphs: Visual cortical neurons often stop increasing their response proportionally as contrast rises. After sustained exposure to strong contrast, their response also shifts toward higher contrast levels. This paper investigates whether two forms of synaptic adaptation, operating at different speeds, can explain these changes within a recurrent network of excitatory spiking neurons.

The fast component is synaptic depression: recently active synapses temporarily become less effective. In the model, this produces response saturation and an advance in response timing at high contrast. The slow component changes the probability that a synapse releases transmitter. Its learning rule is derived by maximizing the mutual information between a neuron's input and output.

Together, these mechanisms explain adaptation in the average membrane potential while allowing the stimulus-modulated component to change only weakly. That distinction connects the proposed mechanism to a specific experimental observation. The authors also propose experiments to estimate effective excitatory feedback and test the synaptic explanation, making the model a source of testable predictions.
neurips-1998-contrast-adaptation-in-simp.tldr: Fast synaptic depression and slower information-maximizing changes in transmitter release jointly explain modeled cortical contrast adaptation.

paragraphs: Hidden Markov models can fit their training examples too closely when there is too little data to estimate all their parameters reliably. This paper addresses that problem by changing the training objective. Alongside fitting the observations, the model is encouraged to maintain a simpler, smoother system of probabilities.

The method adds a penalty to expectation-maximization training. That penalty comes from a mixture of negative exponential distributions assumed to generate the emission probabilities associated with different states. It provides a probabilistic way to constrain complexity during estimation. The authors interpret the method as a generalization of state tying, which controls complexity by sharing parameters across states.

The approach transfers a regularization idea from neural networks to hidden Markov models and demonstrates it in continuous speech recognition. The reported applications improve overfitted triphone models and support speaker adaptation with limited training data. These findings show how restricting the flexibility of probability estimates can be useful both when building detailed speech models and when adapting them from few examples.
neurips-1998-controlling-the-complexity-.tldr: A probabilistic penalty makes HMM training favor simpler models, improving speech modeling and adaptation when training data is scarce.

paragraphs: A population of neurons is often interpreted as collectively representing one value, such as a single motion direction. This paper asks what is lost when decoding is restricted to that interpretation. Neural activity may also express uncertainty or represent several directions at once, particularly when a visual stimulus contains transparent, overlapping motions.

The proposed interpretation treats the population response as encoding a probability distribution over possible values. Decoding finds the distribution that best fits the observed activity. This gives the representation room to express multiple motions as well as uncertainty about them, instead of requiring every activity pattern to resolve into one direction.

The authors apply this framework to psychological and neural studies of motion perception. They report recovery of multiple motions from population responses, something standard approaches do not achieve in the comparison described. The outputs also agree with both successful and mistaken human judgments. This matters because the framework connects richer neural representations to the particular ways perception succeeds and fails.
neurips-1998-distributional-population-c.tldr: Decoding neural activity as a probability distribution recovers multiple motion directions and accounts for both correct and mistaken human judgments.

paragraphs: Generating images of articulated objects from examples is difficult because nearby configurations need not have smoothly changing appearances. A single interpolation model can therefore combine examples in inappropriate ways. This paper addresses the problem by learning several independently smooth appearance mappings, each responsible for a suitable set of examples.

A set-growing procedure identifies clusters that can be approximated well within their convex hull, the region spanned by combinations of those examples. Interpolation is restricted to these accepted sets. The networks may cover overlapping parts of the parameter space, so the method does not require one exclusive partition or one smooth mapping for every possible configuration.

The authors demonstrate the approach with both simulated and real arm images. They report physically valid outputs even where nearby examples look different. The central contribution is a way to decide which examples can safely be interpolated together. This preserves the usefulness of smooth interpolation while accommodating the more complicated appearance changes produced by articulated figures.
neurips-1998-example-based-image-synthes.tldr: Overlapping local interpolation models generate valid articulated-object images where a single smooth appearance model would fail.

paragraphs: The paper studies how people decide whether they have seen a face before. It compares three memory models across three ways of representing faces, producing nine combinations. The target is the probability that a person calls a test face familiar, including cases where familiarity judgments are mistaken.

The models include the Generalized Context Model, a probabilistic sampling model called SimSample, and MMOM, which explicitly represents distinctiveness. The face descriptions use positions in a multidimensional similarity space, projections onto eigenfaces, or responses from Gabor filters. This design examines both the memory computation and the representation on which it operates.

Only MMOM in the multidimensional similarity space predicts the reported familiarity inversion: blends of similar faces can attract more false recognition than many studied faces attract correct recognition. The result supports an account resembling kernel density estimation, where stored faces contribute regions of familiarity. However, the supported account gives distinctive faces broader kernels than typical faces, making distinctiveness essential to explaining the observed judgments.
neurips-1998-facial-memory-is-kernel-den.tldr: A face-memory model that adjusts familiarity kernels for distinctiveness explains why some blended faces seem more familiar than studied faces.

paragraphs: Gaussian process prediction faces a computational obstacle: its cost scales cubically with the number of training examples. The paper investigates how to reduce that burden by expressing an approximate predictor through a finite set of basis functions. This makes the size of the predictive representation an explicit part of the design.

The authors derive optimal finite-dimensional predictors under several assumptions. They compare these predictors with Projected Bayes Regression, a method described as asymptotically optimal, and report superior performance. The comparison matters because optimal behavior in a limiting regime does not by itself establish which approximation is preferable for a particular finite dataset.

The paper also provides a calculation of the minimum model size for a given number of examples. This links the choice of representation size to the amount of available data, alongside the construction of the predictor itself. Numerical experiments support the calculations. Together, the results address both how to approximate a Gaussian process and how large that approximation needs to be.
neurips-1998-finite-dimensional-approxim.tldr: Finite-basis Gaussian process approximations reduce computational demands while providing principled predictors and model-size calculations.

paragraphs: The paper presents a real-time vision system that recognizes actions and interactions as they unfold. It explores two settings: coordinated movements of both hands in Tai Chi and interactions among people in surveillance scenes. Both require interpreting linked movements over time, rather than treating each visible motion as an isolated event.

The system uses a Bayesian framework with feedback between bottom-up visual evidence and top-down interpretations. It compares hidden Markov models with coupled hidden Markov models for representing individual actions and interacting agents. Coupling provides a way to model dependencies between evolving processes. For a fixed amount of training, the coupled models are reported to be more accurate and efficient.

The authors also address limited training data by using synthetic agents to develop prior models of person-to-person interaction. These artificial agents supply expectations about possible interactions that the recognition system can incorporate. The contribution combines temporal modeling, feedback, and simulated behavior to support recognition when observed training examples are limited.
neurips-1998-graphical-models-for-recogn.tldr: A Bayesian vision system uses coupled temporal models and synthetic-agent priors to recognize coordinated human actions and interactions.

paragraphs: A spiking neuron must represent sensory inputs using a limited range of firing rates. This paper studies how a neuron could adapt its own response properties to use that range efficiently. The central idea is to match the response to the statistics of incoming stimuli so that available firing rates are used equally often.

The proposed learning mechanism changes voltage-dependent ionic conductances in Hodgkin-Huxley model neurons. These conductances influence how electrical inputs become spikes, so adapting them changes the information transmitted by the cell. The authors derive an unsupervised, non-Hebbian developmental rule whose objective is to maximize the rate of information transmission.

Under the stated interpretation involving uniform additive noise, an even distribution of firing rates provides efficient use of the neuron's dynamic range. The derived adaptation achieves this equal use within the model. The work therefore identifies the cell's intrinsic electrical properties as adjustable components of sensory coding, connecting stimulus statistics to the development of a neuron's input-output response.
neurips-1998-information-maximization-in.tldr: An information-maximizing learning rule adapts a model neuron's ionic conductances so it uses its available firing rates equally often.

paragraphs: Lazy learning stores examples and waits until a prediction is requested before fitting a local model. It identifies nearby examples using a distance measure and interpolates from those judged relevant. This paper focuses on a consequential choice within that process: how many neighbors to use for each individual query.

The authors propose selecting the neighborhood size from data on a query-by-query basis. They introduce recursive least squares as an efficient tool for identifying and validating candidate local models. This makes model assessment part of the prediction procedure, allowing the amount of nearby evidence used to vary with the location of the query.

The work also explores two ways to use the candidates: selecting a single winning model or combining several promising local models. Evaluation covers six datasets and comparison with a state-of-the-art approach. The contribution is an integrated procedure for constructing, assessing, and selecting local predictions, with both neighborhood size and model combination treated as decisions informed by the available examples.
neurips-1998-lazy-learning-meets-the-rec.tldr: Recursive least squares supports efficient local-model validation and query-specific selection of neighbors for memory-based prediction.

paragraphs: A learning curve describes how average prediction performance changes as a model receives more training data. This paper studies how to calculate such curves for Gaussian process regression. The goal is to understand expected generalization performance across training data, beyond the predictions produced by one particular fitted model.

The analysis begins with an expression for generalization error based on the eigenvalue decomposition of the covariance function. This decomposition provides a mathematical description of the covariance structure that can be used to analyze learning. The author then develops several approximation schemes from that expression and identifies circumstances in which the approximations become exact.

The proposed approximations are compared with existing bounds on Gaussian process learning curves and generally track the true curves substantially more closely. They can also be applied regardless of the input-space dimension. The contribution is therefore a more accurate analytical route from a Gaussian process's covariance specification to its expected learning behavior as training data accumulates.
neurips-1998-learning-curves-for-gaussia.tldr: Covariance eigenvalues yield approximations that more closely describe how Gaussian process regression improves with additional training data.

paragraphs: The paper treats low-level vision as a search for the scene interpretation that best explains observed images. For motion analysis, the hidden scene consists of projected velocities that account for successive frames. For resolution enhancement, the task is to estimate a high-resolution image from lower-resolution observations.

The method learns two kinds of relationships from synthetic data: how image patches relate to scene patches, and how neighboring scene patches relate to one another. The first supplies local evidence about possible interpretations. The second allows the interpretation of one region to be informed by nearby regions, connecting local estimates into a broader scene.

For a new image, the system propagates likelihoods through a Markov network to infer the hidden scene. This computation ignores the effect of loops in the network, an explicit approximation in the method. The authors demonstrate efficient scene estimation for both motion and resolution enhancement, showing how learned local relationships can support different visual inference tasks within one framework.
neurips-1998-learning-to-estimate-scenes.tldr: A Markov network learns relationships among image and scene patches to estimate motion and reconstruct higher-resolution images.

paragraphs: Visual learning can appear highly specific: practice improves performance on a trained stimulus without immediately helping on a new one. This paper revisits that conclusion using moving-dot direction discrimination. It asks whether transfer might be visible in how quickly people learn a new direction, even when their initial performance shows no benefit.

The experiments reproduce the absence of immediate transfer between directions. However, tracking performance over time reveals that the learning rate for the new direction doubles. A second experiment also reproduces transfer after training with easy stimuli. These observations distinguish two benefits of prior practice: starting a new task better and improving at it faster.

The authors interpret both patterns through signal detection theory with limited computational resources. Their account produces direct transfer and changes in learning rate as task difficulty increases. This provides a common explanation for results previously associated with different learning processes or visual areas, and shows why measuring only immediate performance can overlook a meaningful form of generalization.
neurips-1998-mechanisms-of-generalizatio.tldr: Visual practice can generalize by doubling learning speed on a new motion direction even when immediate performance does not improve.

paragraphs: The paper derives an exact account of how a perceptron changes during online Hebbian learning with a restricted training set. Online learning updates the model as examples are presented, making the evolution of learning itself the object of study. The analysis considers a regime where the training-set size grows linearly with the number of inputs.

The solution covers both noiseless and noisy teachers, allowing the dynamics to be examined with and without noise in the teaching signal. Its value lies in providing an exact mathematical reference for this specified setting. A theory of restricted-data learning can therefore be checked against a case whose evolution has already been solved.

The authors explicitly state that their calculation does not extend to non-Hebbian learning rules. This defines its role as a benchmark for broader theories rather than a solution for every update rule. More general methods can be assessed by whether they reproduce this known case, making a narrowly solvable model useful for developing wider accounts of learning dynamics.
neurips-1998-on-line-learning-with-restr.tldr: An exact solution for online Hebbian perceptron learning provides a benchmark for theories of learning from restricted training sets.

paragraphs: This paper studies how to adapt an acoustic transient classifier to the dedicated hardware that runs it. The starting point is a previously proposed correlation algorithm that has already been implemented and demonstrated in a mixed-mode architecture. The new work investigates algorithm variants intended to improve classification on that chosen hardware.

The variants change several parts of the computation. Time-channel and frequency-channel differencing alter how changes in the input are represented. Input and output normalization adjust the values entering and leaving the classifier. Other variants concern how template values are trained and converted to binary form, making the template representation itself part of the optimization.

These choices matter because the performance of a dedicated VLSI system depends on the algorithm implemented within it. The paper therefore treats representation, normalization, and template design as connected hardware-facing decisions. Its stated contribution is an investigation of those alternatives for acoustic transient classification, with the objective of finding the best classification behavior for an already selected processing architecture.
neurips-1998-optimizing-correlation-algo.tldr: The paper explores differencing, normalization, and template design to optimize an acoustic transient classifier for dedicated VLSI hardware.

paragraphs: The paper analyzes Hopfield-type networks that store sequences of patterns near their capacity limit. Their interactions are asymmetric, which violates detailed balance and prevents the use of an equilibrium statistical-mechanics analysis. Understanding sequence recall therefore requires a direct treatment of how the network evolves through time.

Using generating functional methods, the authors derive exact closed equations in the infinite-system limit. These describe sequence overlap, correlations, and responses: quantities tracking recall and temporal behavior. Stationary cycling solutions lead to a phase diagram that characterizes the network's regimes. The analysis also finds that an effective delayed self-interaction present in symmetric models disappears here.

The authors connect that disappearance to a larger storage capacity, approximately 0.269 compared with approximately 0.139 for Hopfield networks storing static patterns. Extensive computer simulations agree closely with the theory. The result shows how the dynamics associated with asymmetric sequence storage can change capacity, while providing an exact large-system framework for analyzing recall near saturation.
neurips-1998-phase-diagram-and-storage-c.tldr: An exact dynamical analysis links asymmetric sequence storage to increased capacity in Hopfield-type neural networks.

paragraphs: Different imaging sensors provide different observations of the same scene. This paper combines those observations by explicitly modeling how they were formed. It assumes that each sensor image is a noisy, locally linear function of an underlying true scene, making image fusion a problem of estimating that shared hidden scene.

Within a Bayesian framework, the authors obtain either maximum-likelihood or maximum-a-posteriori scene estimates. The former seeks the scene that best explains the observations; the latter also incorporates prior information. Both follow from the same image-formation model, giving the combination of sensor measurements a probabilistic interpretation.

Estimating the image-formation parameters uses local second-order image statistics, connecting the method to local principal component analysis. This means the fusion procedure draws on statistical relationships within image regions. Demonstrations combine visible-band and infrared images. The contribution is a unified way to describe sensor noise, estimate relationships among observations, and reconstruct a scene from multiple imaging sources.
neurips-1998-probabilistic-image-sensor-.tldr: A probabilistic image-formation model combines noisy sensor images into a shared scene estimate, demonstrated with visible and infrared imagery.

paragraphs: The paper proposes training trading systems by directly optimizing financial objectives through reinforcement learning. The objectives include profit or wealth, the Sharpe ratio, and a differential Sharpe ratio designed for online learning. This makes the chosen financial measure part of the learning target rather than leaving trading performance separate from training.

The work extends an earlier comparison with supervised learning by comparing Q-learning with the authors' Recurrent Reinforcement Learning algorithm. The comparison examines alternative reinforcement-learning approaches within the same trading problem. Including several financial objectives also makes clear that the desired behavior depends on what measure the system is trained to improve.

New simulations report predictability in monthly S&P 500 index data over the 25-year period from 1970 through 1994. The authors also use sensitivity analysis to obtain economic insight into the trader's structure. Together, these contributions connect direct financial optimization, algorithm comparison, and interpretation of the learned trader within the historical simulation setting studied.
neurips-1998-reinforcement-learning-for-.tldr: Trading systems learn directly from financial objectives, with Q-learning and recurrent reinforcement learning compared in historical market simulations.

paragraphs: The order in which a block of computer instructions executes can substantially affect its running time. The paper notes that different schedules can produce differences of a factor of two or more. Compilers therefore rely on scheduling heuristics suited to particular processor implementations, but developing those heuristics requires considerable time and expense.

The authors investigate rollouts and reinforcement learning as ways to construct scheduling heuristics for basic blocks of straight-line code. Both approaches address the decision process involved in choosing an instruction order. Their purpose is to obtain useful scheduling behavior through computational methods, reducing reliance on the costly construction of architecture-specific heuristics.

The reported results distinguish the two approaches: the rollout scheduler outperforms a commercial scheduler, while the reinforcement-learning scheduler performs almost as well as that commercial system. These findings show that automatically constructed scheduling strategies can be competitive in the studied setting. They also identify rollouts as the stronger of the two reported alternatives in that comparison.
neurips-1998-scheduling-straight-line-co.tldr: Automatically constructed instruction schedulers prove competitive, with rollouts beating a commercial scheduler and reinforcement learning approaching its performance.

paragraphs: The paper introduces a support vector regression algorithm that adapts the width of a tube around its predictions. The tube describes a band within which data points are accommodated. Its central design choice is to let the user specify an allowed fraction of points outside that band, while the algorithm adjusts the radius.

For the chosen fraction, the method finds a flexible tube of minimum radius subject to the stated bound on outside points. This connects the fitted tolerance directly to the data and to an interpretable user-selected constraint. The resulting learning problem jointly concerns the regression fit and how tightly its surrounding band can enclose the observations.

The authors also show how to use parametric tube shapes whose radius is not constant. This extends the construction beyond a band with the same width everywhere. The algorithm receives both theoretical and experimental analysis. Its contribution is a regression formulation that learns the tube size automatically while allowing structured variation in its shape.
neurips-1998-shrinking-the-tube-a-new-su.tldr: A support vector regression algorithm learns a minimal-width prediction tube from a user-chosen bound on the fraction of points outside it.

paragraphs: Sparse coding represents data using components that are strongly active only rarely. This paper uses that property to separate meaningful structure from noise. The starting assumption is that the underlying components have non-Gaussian distributions and are observed after contamination by Gaussian noise, giving denoising a statistical estimation formulation.

The authors derive a nonlinear shrinkage operation through maximum-likelihood estimation. Applied to the sparse representation, this operation reduces noise in the component values. They also show how to choose a sparse coding basis specifically for denoising, so the method addresses both the representation of the data and the transformation applied within that representation.

The approach is closely related to wavelet shrinkage, but learns both its features and its shrinkage parameters directly from the data. That combination is the principal stated benefit over wavelet methods. The contribution connects sparse representation learning with a noise-removal rule derived from probability models, allowing the denoising procedure to adapt its components and their treatment together.
neurips-1998-sparse-code-shrinkage-denoi.tldr: Sparse-code denoising learns both a representation and nonlinear shrinkage parameters from data using a probabilistic noise model.

paragraphs: The paper asks how learning based on individual spike correlations differs from learning described through average firing rates. It formulates a correlation-based synaptic learning rule at the spike level and analyzes its dynamics mathematically. The aim is to identify effects of precise spike timing that matter for the development of synaptic structure.

The derivation assumes that learning and spiking occur on separable timescales, allowing a differential equation for the slower learning dynamics. For a linear Poisson neuron receiving time-dependent stochastic input, the analysis shows that correlations on a millisecond timescale affect learning. Fine temporal relationships therefore contribute to the model's behavior.

Correlations between input and output spikes tend to stabilize structure formation when the learning window has a form consistent with Hebb's principle. The paper also discusses conditions under which the average synaptic weight normalizes intrinsically. These results connect the timing dependence of a learning rule to the stability and regulation of the synaptic organization it produces.
neurips-1998-spike-based-compared-to-rat.tldr: A mathematical comparison shows that millisecond spike correlations can stabilize Hebbian structure formation under suitable learning-window conditions.

paragraphs: The paper studies how shared noise affects the accuracy of a neural population representing an angle in two dimensions. Each neuron responds broadly around its preferred orientation. Activity fluctuations are modeled as Gaussian noise, with correlations between neuron pairs decreasing exponentially as their preferred orientations become farther apart.

The authors calculate Fisher information to assess how precisely the population can encode the angle. In the parameter regime they identify as biologically relevant, positive correlations reduce estimation capability compared with an uncorrelated population. Adding neurons does not necessarily overcome this problem: sufficiently strong positive correlations cause the information to approach a finite ceiling as population size grows.

Negative correlations have the opposite reported effect, substantially increasing the population's information capacity. The findings show that encoding accuracy depends on the structure and sign of shared variability, alongside the number of available neurons. Within this specified noise model, correlations determine whether a larger population continues to provide useful information or encounters a limiting ceiling.
neurips-1998-the-effect-of-correlations-.tldr: In a modeled neural population, positive noise correlations reduce angular information and can impose a ceiling, while negative correlations increase it.

paragraphs: Internet traffic routing involves interacting decisions whose combined effects determine network performance. This paper studies a collective intelligence, or COIN: a collection of reinforcement-learning algorithms designed so that their joint behavior improves a global utility function. The design target is therefore the performance of the interacting system as a whole.

The authors summarize the theory behind COINs and apply it to constructing routing controllers. Automated design is central to the definition: the learning algorithms are organized with the global objective in view. This provides a way to approach routing as a coordinated learning problem, where the value of a decision is connected to collective behavior.

Experiments indicate that the resulting COINs outperform all previously investigated reinforcement-learning shortest-path routing algorithms in the reported comparison. The finding supports the usefulness of designing interacting learners around a shared system objective. The contribution combines a general account of collective learning with a concrete routing application in which the quality of the collective decisions can be evaluated.
neurips-1998-using-collective-intelligen.tldr: Routing experiments favor interacting reinforcement learners designed around global utility over previously investigated reinforcement-learning shortest-path methods.

paragraphs: The paper presents a compact, low-power vision chip that rapidly locates the center of detected motion. It performs this processing at the focal plane and models functions associated with the retina and superior colliculus. The intended application is fast, lightweight autonomous vehicles that need visual information for navigation.

Mixed-signal CMOS circuitry combines photodetection, edge detection, onset detection, and centroid localization. The localization stage receives asynchronously triggered row and column address events within a time window. Two linear resistive grids then produce analog coordinates for the motion centroid, converting distributed detection events into a spatial location.

This arrangement connects several stages of visual processing within a dedicated circuit, yielding a compact motion-location signal that can support vehicle behavior. The chip is used to realize autonomous navigation, and the paper discusses a line-following algorithm that also avoids obstacles. Its contribution brings together biologically motivated sensing, event-driven localization, and a navigation application in one hardware implementation.
neurips-1998-vlsi-implementation-of-moti.tldr: A compact mixed-signal vision chip converts motion events into centroid coordinates for lightweight autonomous navigation.
